Copper Long-term Outlook 

# Executive summary 

As we move through the year and more trade and production data becomes available we get a much better feel of how demand is progressing.  With first half data now available for most countries and regions it has become necessary to make changes to our estimates of consumption in 2011, with most of these changes being negative.  The key exception to this is China, where we have significantly upgraded our view of demand after a thorough review of changes in hidden stocks, which has revealed much stronger demand than apparent consumption figures alone would suggest.  This change has added c200kt to lift Chinese demand to 7.78Mt, representing growth of 8% over 2010.  Meanwhile, it would be easy to ascribe downgrades in much of the rest of the world to the worsening economic environment in the final part of the year, however, we had already been forecasting weaker activity in H2 and as such, our lower estimates are mainly a function of sluggish consumption in the year to date.  The net effect of these changes has been to lower global growth to 4.6% from 5.4% in our previous quarterly report, amounting to some 20.17Mt of metal. 

Conversely, the supply side of the market has done better than our previous projections and despite a number of recent high profile strikes, the level of disruptions to date is still in line with our 5% allowance.  We have increased our estimate of refined output this year to 19.951Mt from 19.840Mt in our Q2 report.  Inevitably, a lower estimate of demand but a stronger expectation of production has had an impact on our market balance, reducing the deficit for this year from -465 in our last report to -217 now.  As we noted above, our lower demand estimate for this year is not directly related to the tumultuous economic backdrop amid seemingly never ending debt crises, however, ironically, much of the collapse in copper prices has been on fears over the outlook for demand.  These concerns, in addition to a flight away from so called “risk” assets has resulted in lower average prices through the third quarter and as a consequence has lowered our 2011 price estimate to US$9140/t ($4.15/lb) from US$9586/t ($4.35/lb) in our June report. 

Overall base case mine production capability is forecast to decline by 0.7% p.a. between 2010 and 2025 with output falling from a peak of ~20.3Mt in 2015 to ~14.6Mt in 2025.  For this year, demand for mine production will exceed available base case supply by the almost 300kt, lower than our Q2 forecast of almost 500kt.  We expect this market to turn closer to balance in 2012, but in 2013 the new material from projects under construction will likely tip this balance into surplus. 

Our smelter production forecast for 2011 now stands at 15.5Mt which is 6.4% higher than was the case in 2010.  Copperin-concentrates contributed an estimated 86% (89% in 20

09) of overall smelter output last year with the balance derived from scrap and purchased blister.  Average primary smelter capacity utilisation rates should exceed 87% this year, up from 83% in 2010.  Overall, we expect 4.36Mt/a of new smelting capacity to be set up over the forecast period. 

The majority of the revisions made to our smelter production capability forecasts are largely reflected in the changes to our refinery output estimates and these can be seen in the main report.  Taking these into account, base case global copper refined production _capability_ is now expected to reach 20.25Mt/a in 2011 (+6.3%), 22.6Mt/a in 2012 (+11.5%) and 24.4Mt/a in 2013 (+8.2%).  However, growth is forecast to slow markedly in 2014-2015, and then to decline from 2016 onwards.  As a consequence, overall global capability will increase by only 1.3% p.a. between 2010 and 2025.  In tonnage terms this equates to an increase of ~4.06Mt to 23.1Mt in 2025. 

We remain of the view that the market will return to balance next year, although a smaller than previously forecast deficit for 2011 has resulted in production having less ground to make up to match supply with demand and as a consequence, we now forecast a small surplus.  A softer forecast for demand growth the following year, in addition to an improved starting point of a surplus rather than the prior deficit results in an ever greater imbalance and we now anticipate a surplus of 421kt in 2013.  Despite moving back into balance in 2012, the market will remain fundamentally tight, with stock days set to average 48, compared to 50 this year and as such, prices will remain well supported.  By 2013, the surplus that we discuss above will lift average stock days upwards, to 53 days and as a consequence, there will be downward pressure on prices.  We now forecast 2012 prices to average US$9207/t ($4.18/lb) in 2011$, with prices peaking in the second quarter before ebbing lower thereafter, while 2013’s forecast average price is now expected to be US$8110/t ($3.68/lb). 

Any extended period of low copper prices will serve to discourage companies to develop new mines or expand existing operations.  This projected period of low prices between 2014-2017 will result in a turnaround in the market’s fortunes between 2019 and 2020.  During these years prices are expected to rise sharply, reaching a cycle high of $7055-7275/t ($3.20-3.30/lb) in constant 2011$ through the period to 2025. 

Our long-term incentive price remains unchanged at $2.50/lb in current dollars over the period to 2025.  This has been derived from our analysis of mine project incentive prices and projected demand for mine production over this period, although we have made no allowance for potential mining-specific inflation which could further increase this forecast.

# Demand analysis 

## Overview 

**Pace of demand growth slows earlier than exp

ected** We have made a number of changes to our demand forecasts for this year since our last quarterly publication. Of particular note is a significant upgrade to Chinese consumption on the basis of detailed analysis of hidden stock changes, although this has been offset by decreases in our estimates of European and North American demand. Given the negative economic backdrop it might appear that the downgrades were directly related to weaker expectations for activity in the second half of the year. However, they were as much a result of having full first half data to had as we had already forecast a weakening into H2. To an extent, the changes outlined above net each other out, although we have lowered our global demand growth estimate for this year to 4.6%, from 5.4% last quarter. Changes to the survey population of semis producers have certainly muddied the waters but looking past the numbers in isolation, it is difficult to argue against the strength in Chinese demand, particularly given the buoyancy of some key end use sectors. Meanwhile, premia remain firm, while imports have maintained an upward bent even in the face of negative arbitrage on occasion. **Industrial activity eases back as inflation begins to edge lower** The latest release of industrial production data revealed that activity has slowed modestly in line with authorities’ aims to slow price inflation. Engineering a soft landing is easier said than done but price increases have begun to slow, with the latest figures showing CPI up by 6.2% in August after hitting 6.5% the previous month. One swallow doesn’t make a summer of course but this decline fits with our view of easing inflation in the final part of the year. Controlling prices is the easy part but controlling prices without s

lowing industrial activity too sharply is more difficult.  However.  August’s 13.5% hike in industrial production is broadly in line with our view of full year IP growth.  Overall, data releases suggest an end to the tightening cycle in China, particularly when set against the backdrop of concerns over the health of major economies in Europe and North America. 

**Arbitrage is favourable but demand drives imports** From April the price differential between SHFE and LME material favoured importing material, although imports of cathode into China continued to flag until May before beginning to improve the following month.  The lag should not be surprising given the distances that material typically has to be shipped.  The arbitrage window closed again in June and July while imports continued to enjoy month on month gains, even if the year-on-year comparisons were still deeply in the red.  Significantly, preliminary data for imports in August indicate that they have maintained their upward streak.  Given that imports continued to improve despite the negative arbitrage when these orders would have been placed implies that these orders were placed because of healthy demand and not simply to make a quick buck on the SHFE/LME price differential.  Several other developments support this view and we reiterate our expectations of solid H2 import figures. 

**Lack of contango dancing to the same tune** That the Shanghai futures market was in backwardation and not contango in four of the past five months comparing the front month to the three month contract is indicative of scarcity of material.  At the time of writing front month prices remain dearer, which supports our view of a tight Chinese market and that domestic demand is driving cathode imports.  Meanwhile, premia remain at elevated levels providing further evidence of the health of Chinese consumption.

**Scrap spreads favour refined metal** A further argument in support of firm demand for refined material in the second half of the year is the relative scarcity of scrap metal presently.  Scrap spreads are extremely tight at the moment and there are even reports of cleaner grades trading at a premium to refined metal.  As such, semis producers are purchasing cathode and the direct use of scrap at semis producers is suffering as a result. 

**Stock levels broadly unchanged** The one element of the demand picture that doesn’t reflect strong demand is the direction of stocks.  Inventories on exchange have edged higher since the end of the second quarter, although not by much, while bonded warehouse stocks are now at a base level where much of what is in there is not necessarily available for sale.  We do expect bonded warehouse stock levels to edge higher during the third quarter by around 100kt as inevitably some of the increasing imports will at least temporarily find their way into bonded warehouse

s, although we forecast that this will reverse itself in the fourth quarter.  The other element to stock levels are those within the supply chain and at copper consumers, which have been increasing modestly of late as semis producers opportunistically restock on price dips. 

**Detailed analysis of stock movements leads to demand upgrade** A detailed review of first half data has led to an upgrade in our estimate of full year growth in China this year.  Looking at apparent consumption statistics alone, without consideration of unreported stock movements, fails to take into account the significant stock changes that typically take place in China through the year.  Indeed, it is a much shallower stock build in China in the first quarter this year than took place in 2010 that has resulted in real demand rising by 7.3% in Q1 by our estimates.  When stripping out stock movements this would have been a contraction of around 6% in the same period.  This was also a feature of second quarter demand data, with real demand estimated to have grown by some 13.8%, compared to a simple apparent consumption calculation which reveals an 8% contraction.  For the full year we now expect growth in refined copper consumption of 8% in 2011, with a further 8% increase the following year.  For the period 2010-2025 we remain of the view that demand growth will average between 5 and 6% per year.

**Automotive market in consolidation mode** 2011 is a year of consolidation for the Chinese auto industry after two years of rapid expansion in vehicle sales and production.  Although disruptions caused by the Japanese earthquake have had an impact on Chines

e vehicle production, the slowdown has primarily been caused by the Chinese consumer. Vehicle sales began to slow after the expiration of incentive schemes at the turn of the year, and policies introduced in some major cities to limit new vehicle registrations have not helped. In addition, higher fuel prices have dented consumer sentiment towards buying a car. As a result, total vehicle sales growth slowed to 3.8% year on year during the first half of the year, down from 33% in 2010. As a result of this relatively sluggish pace of demand by Chinese standards, we do not expect vehicle production growth in excess of 5% this year. **Affordable homes target cut for 2012** China has reportedly cut its target for the construction of affordable homes to be built next year to 8 million. Previously, plans were to build 36m affordable homes by 2015, including 10m this year and in 2012. On the face of it this should be negative for demand growth next year, but we do not expect this to cause any major downturn in consumption of copper from the sector. Indeed, construction activity has maintained a strong pace this year and given the lag between construction starts and copper use in buildings, this year’s strength will likely sustain copper demand well into next year. However, we maintain our previously stated view that the disconnect between housing starts and completions points to a slowdown in construction activity at some point. While the US economy appeared to be improving during the earlier months of the year, copper demand also benefited and remained pretty healthy, especially in the wire markets. But following the renewed discussion over the wider global economic downturn which started in May, the previous hesitation seen at the buying level has worsened to a halt. After showing 14 month-on-month improvements out of 15 during the February 2010-April 2011 period, total US wire rod shipments, according to data from the American Bureau of Metal Statistics (ABMS), contracted in July for the third straight month. As noted, July is indeed traditionally weak, but the 14% drop in both shipments and production this July compared to the same month in 2010 illustrates just how lifeless the market seems to be. This was, in fact, the worst monthly fall since Q4 2009. Furthermore, ABMS data show that rod held in stock grew to 31.3kt this July, from 28.6kt a month prior and from July 2010’s 23.8kt. **CBSA members’ shipments also fall** Copper rod and alloy product shipments by members of the distributors’ association, the CBSA, mirror the mills’ performance. Although a much smaller market segment, CBSA member shipments still account for between 10-15% of the national market. Their shipments were down in July by 9.5% monthon-month, but only marginally down on the comparable January-July period; however, the feeling is that already the best of the year is behind us. **But Russian material continues to flood in** That said, domestic rod producers, despite having reduced their output schedules to match sales, are also continuing to face high imports from Russia. These came about from May, largely entering Baltimore and New Orleans ports, and have been the direct consequence of the Russian government placing an export tax on cathode from last December. The cathodes have remained at home to be converted domestically, then exported as rod, tariff-free. Russian rod producers began by exporting to southern Europe, then turned to what at the time, back in May, were resurgent rod markets in the USA. Ameri

can traders and distributors have clearly absorbed the lower-priced Russian imports, leaving US rod producers to respond in the only manner possible in the short term, which has been to reduce output themselves.  So far, there is no talk publicly of the domestics heading for protectionist measures from Washington D.C., but should the market not pick up noticeably into the fourth quarter, we would expect to see some action by the mills in order to protect what should be the typically strongest period in 2012. 

**US forecast copper demand in the near term downgraded…** In light of the deteriorating market conditions since May, we have reduced slightly our expectations for copper demand in the US for this year and into 2012.  Now we are forecasting 1.813Mt _vs_ 1.841Mt in our last report for this year, and 1.782Mt vs 1.821Mt for 2012, with similar reductions for the years beyond. 

**..and yet new investments show defiance against unfavourable sector conditions** While it is somewhat easier to issue the general comment that first-use copper demand will fall away over the long term in the USA, as in all first world countries, there are some developments afoot which run counter to these expectations.   In particular, there have been two developments in the US rod sector this year which should see new capacity brought on line this year and in 2013.  In the middle of the summer, Peruvian rod manufacturer, Tecnofil, bought New York-based Sherburne Metals Co., and it is the new owner’s intention to re-start the 30kt/a UpCast oxygen-free rod line from October.  A second, 15kt/a horizontal caster will not receive re-commissioning assistance from UpCast personnel because it is a modified line, rather than original equipment, and Tecnofil has yet to state its intentions with it.  Earlier, in April, Steel Dynamics Inc (SDI) announced a joint venture with Spain’s LaFarga group to invest in a 200kt/a capacity rod mill using Properzi technology. The line will primarily use scrap feed, with SDI’s subsidiary, OmniSource, being well-placed to provide much of the raw material. 

Although the SDI line will make a rod product that can target “only” around 80% of wire markets because of quality reasons, it still represents a considerable new chunk of capacity into a sector that has seen a fair degree of contraction over the past decade.  In 2008, Freeport closed its 180kt/a capacity Chicago mill and Superior Essex shuttered its 53kt/a Vincennes, IN plant.  The example of Sherburne’s 45kt/a capacity from its two rod lines being temporarily closed through bankruptcy during most of 2010 through to this month illustrates the difficulties that the sector has been having in recent years.

## Europe 

**Debt crisis won’t go away** Debt issues continue to plague the European economy and although it is not entirely clear whether this will have a direct impact on industrial activity in the short term, the impact will likely come at some stage through the transmission mechanism of weaker consumer confidence and then spending.  For now though, it would appear that export markets continue to support industrial output, even though we expect softening through the final part of the year, which will feed through into softer demand for copper. 

**Second half slowdown comes early** With most of the data in for the first half it has become apparent that second quarter demand was weaker than we had initially expected and has resulted in a downgrade to expectations of cathode demand that we discuss later.  We always had forecast slowing activity in the second half of the year but it would appear from apparent consumption calculations and company releases that this slowdown came a little earlier than anticipated.

**Wire rod loses its shine** Wire rod production data from major European semis producer Aurubis confirms the view outlined above, with their output down by 5.7% year on year in the second quarter of calendar year, although this was offset to a degree by increased output of shapes, which grew by 10% in the same period.  Previously, wire rod had been one of the stronger segments in Europe, although a key factor in the European market this year has been a sharp increase in Russian wire rod exports, which the market was able to accommodate earlier in the year but perhaps couldn’t in the second quarter.  Notably, from May, imports of rod into America from Russia began to increase supporting the view of a slowing European market, with Russian producers shipping output elsewhere. 

**Italian semis output slips in Q2** It is not possible to say the extent of the real impact on demand from the ongoing European debt crisis in general and in Italy in particular but whatever the cause, Italian semis production fell in the second quarter.  Output of copper semis slipped 4.9%, while copper alloy semis production contracted by a lesser 1% to leave total copper and copper alloy semis down by 3.1% overall, compared to a 1% expansion in the first quarter. # Trends in consumption of secondary copper 

## Scrap definition 

Copper scrap is classified into two general categories called old and new scrap.  New scrap, or manufacturing scrap, is generated during the fabrication of copper products and returned to the mill for reprocessing, or sold, and is not considered a new source of copper supply.  A manufacturer may generate up to 60% of scrap as clippings, trimmings, stampings, borings, and turnings when processing copper and copper-base products into finished articles.  New scrap is termed "run-around" or home scrap (which does not enter the scrap statistics) when it is generated internally at the plant re-using it, or it may be called "purchased return scrap" when returned by a customer from a plant external to that purchasing and re-using it.  Old scrap is generated from worn out, discarded or obsolete copper products and thus, is considered to be a “new” source of supply. 

## Scrapping rates 

The availability of _old_ copper scrap is linked to the volume of copper-containing products installed/purchased and their life cycles, or duration.  The life of copper in electrical equipment and machinery averages 30-35 years; in non-electrical machinery, 15 years; in housing, 35-75 years; in transportation, 10 years; in all other sectors, about 10 years.  The average for the industry is estimated to be 15-20 years.  The rate of (old) scrap recovery and its availability to be the market is limited not only by copper's long life, but also by the sensitivity of scrap collection rates to market prices. 

Over the past 20 years, the volume of _new_ copper scrap has not grown in line with industrial consumption of copper because manufacturing efficiencies have improved, leading to as much as a 50% fall in new scrap generation over the period. 

## Scrap usage 

Most old scrap recovered from the market place must be reprocessed either by smelting and refining, or, to a lesser extent, by leaching and electrowinning to form a pure copper product.  Fire refining in a reverberatory or other furnace may be sufficient for the better grades of scrap.  This latter process uses oxidation, fluxing and reduction, with a refined ingot, wire bar, slab, or billet usually being the end product. 

Certain products, such as brass rod (manufactured using 80-90% scrap) can contain higher amounts of scrap than others while still maintaining product quality tolerance.  Others, such as wire rod, must contain far less impurities (typically 5%) since these could affect the drawability (leading to snapping) of the wire rod in producing wire.  New scrap is readily used by brass and copper tube mills to generate new semi-fabricated forms with little additional treatment. Because minimal clean-up procedures are needed, this type of scrap is commonly called "direct melt", or No.1 scrap.  In general, No. 1 scrap is contained in copper and copper-alloy products, rather tha

n wire rod.  Scrap purchases by brass mills are based primarily on activity levels at the mills and the relative price differential between cathode and No. 1 scrap, rather than the actual copper price.  When business conditions are strong, brass mills have access to large volumes of return scrap.  When manufacturing (and, possibly imports) decline, mills may be forced to increase their cathode purchases. 

Low copper prices over the period 1997-2003 led to a reduction in the availability of smelting and refining grade scrap with a corresponding decline in the processing of this material in countries such the USA and in Europe.  The notable exception has been China where there has been an upward trend in the treatment of smelting and refining grade scrap material.  Economic and environmental considerations have also played a major role, with the cost of environmental compliance often leading to plant closures, particularly in the USA.  This is despite the fact that the cost of recovering one tonne of copper from scrap is approximately half that of recovery through the conventional route (concentratesmelting-refining).  Secondary smelters and ingot markers typically consume the lion's share (90%) of No.2 scrap and most of the auto radiators and red brass scrap. 

## Scrap consumption 

Copper produced from scrap (at smelters, refineries and in direct use) amounted to 8.36Mt in 2010, an increase of 15.8% on the prior year and accounting for 35% of copper consumed.  Direct use scrap took the lions share, representing some 58% of copper produced from scrap, with smelters (25%) and refineries (18%) producing copper from the balance. 

Scrap use posted a strong recovery in 2010, after contraction in the previous two years as declining copper prices resulted in a lack of incentive to collect scrap while sluggish industrial production meant limited scrap generation. Quarterly prices sometimes approaching $10,000/t over the period to 2012 reflect tightness in the market following a period of producer reticence to invest when capital costs were high (2007-2008) followed by a collapse of the availability of funding from late 2008 into 2009.  The combination of abnormal supply shortages coupled with a massive pull on demand from China and increased fund appetite has resulted in prices moving in excess of levels that ordinarily would be required to maintain an orderly market.  Over the period to 2025 we would expect fundamental support for prices to be somewhat lower as described below. 

**Incentive pricing provides the most appropriate estimate of long-term average prices** For industries such as copper that are in structural deficit, that is, with long-term demand significantly in excess of base case production intentions, we are of the opinion that while there are various techniques used by the industry to project long-term copper prices, _incentive pricing_ provides the most appropriate estimate of long-term cycle average prices. 

The incentive price analysis examines the price required to provide an investor a given rate of return for each project, and calculates the price required in theory to warrant investment in sufficient cumulative capacity to meet potential demand.  In this context long-term can be considered the cycle average price over the next cycle, i.e. the decade over which a project would expect to see payback. 

**Our project incentive price over the period to 2025 is $2.50/lb, but could move higher** In terms of long-term average prices, these are critically dependant upon the metal demand outlook and on capital and operating costs.  The incentive price methodology starts by estimating the demand for additional mine capacity after allowing for scrap usage and base case mine production changes.  Critically, in a demand growth scenario involving depleting mines, the demand for additional capacity increases with time and care must be exercised in precisely defining the forecast period over

Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - September 2011 Page 30 of 33 Copper Long-term Outlook # Principle uses of copper Copper consumption can be divided into three main product groups which are copper wire rod, copper products and copper alloy products. Copper wire rod, which accounts for an estimated 55% of total Global consumption (i.e. including scrap) and ~70% of primary consumption, is copper’s main first use. With the exception of silver, copper has the highest electrical conductivity of all the metals. This helps to explain why the principal application for copper wire rod is wire and cable. Wire rod is consumed in five main wire and cable markets which include general and industrial cable, utility power cable, telecommunication cable, other insulated wire and winding wire. In general, wire and cable and copper products are consumed in five broad sectors: construction, electric and electronic products, industrial machinery and equipment, transportation equipment and consumer and general products. Of these, construction is the largest sector for consuming copper, accounting for 33% of total copper consumption. The main wire and cable and copper products consumed in the construction industry include building wire, power cable, copper plumbing and air condition

ing tube, copper sheet and alloy products. 

Building wire is the largest of the wire and cable markets, accounting for ~35% of wire rod consumption.  Rising intensity of use, in both the mature and developing economies, will be largely responsible for building wire maintaining this position.  The number of electrical appliances used at home and at the workplace continues to rise, particularly in the mature economies, thereby leading to an increase in the number of power outlets needed per building.  In addition, recent technical issues imply that more copper wire and cable will be needed in the future.  One of these issues, electrical energy efficiency involves using less power to perform a given task by using more or heavier copper conductors.  Finally, good power quality, defined as the uninterrupted, undistorted flow of electricity at the correct voltage, is also helping to drive up the demand for building wire due to higher power quality being achieved by installing additional circuits and heavier wires and cables. 

In contrast to the building and industrial cable market, the power utility market is the smallest of all the wire and cable segments.  However, demand growth for power cable will be supported by both the general recovery in utility investment and the fact that copper, the mainstay of power grids worldwide, still has considerable potential to carry energy better and reduce losses than aluminium. 

Copper tube, which accounts for an estimated 13% of global refined copper consumption, is the largest of the copper product markets.  The two main uses are in plumbing and heating systems and in air conditioners and refrigeration (ACR tube).  The steady proliferation of plumbing amenities in and around the home, particularly as many houses built today within the mature economies have more than one bathroom, are largely responsible for copper plumbing tube demand growth.  Elsewhere, improved living standards in the developing economies, leading to higher demand for air conditioners, continues to boost demand for ACR tube.  This is particularly the case in China and India where improved power supply will lead to a surge in the consumption of air conditioners over the coming years.  Meanwhile in the mature economies, the market is being driven by external factors such as environmental issues, regulatory concerns and social demands for comfort. 

Other copper and copper alloy products consumed by the construction sector include copper sheet and strip, rods, bars and sections plus brass products.  Copper sheet is used for roofing, eaves gutters, drain pipes for rainwater and lining for facades, while rods bars and sections, along with brass products, are used for building fixture and fittings.  In hospitals, brass doorknobs and push plates are widely used because it has been proven that they help to reduce cross contamination. 

Electrical and electronic products are copper’s second largest consuming sector, accounting for 33% of total coppe

r demand.  Copper containing electrical and electronic products include telecommunication cable, power cable, transformer windings, semiconductors and motors for heavy appliances. 

Since the early 1990s copper telecommunication cable has been largely substituted by fibre optic cable in long distance networks.  However, owing to its high cost, copper telecom cable has remained the preferred link between the main network and consumers.  In addition, the development of the internet and e-mail has further enhanced the role of copper in telecommunications in recent years.  The need for information to be carried quicker along the telecommunication network has led to the introduction of asymmetrical digital subscriber line technology (ADSL).  The ADSL is a dedicated circuit between a home and the telephone company’s central office that uses normal copper telephone lines.  The addition of an ADSL chip to the existing copper network means that users can download files around 15 times faster than an analogue dial-up connection. 

Dramatic gains in copper consumption to have occurred within the home because of a system known to the telecommunications industry as ‘structured wiring’.  The cable carrying voice, computer and television signals is connected to a central hub in the home.  Individual cables then run independently from here to high-quality connections in rooms throughout the house.  Cables connected to the hub consist of four pairs of twisted wires, capable of carrying more electronic signals with less interference and resistance than the older four-stranded telephone wires. High-speed digital service lines now provide computer data transmission 50 to 270 times faster than that of the fastest dial-up modem connected to a telephone line.  More importantly, with the number of homes connected to the Internet and usage continuing to increase strongly, demand for higher quality copper telecommunication wire and cable is expected to surge in the coming years. 

The other main wire and cable segment to supply the electrical sector is winding wire.  Winding wire demand accounts for an estimated 20% of copper wire rod consumption, making it the third largest wire and cable market.  Applications include transformers, generators, stereos, television sets and motors.  Indeed, it is the need to improve electrical efficiency of this last application, particularly in the matu

re economies, that has generated the most growth in winding wire demand recently.  This is because improved electrical efficiency involves using a larger conductor in order to reduce electrical resistance, as well as ensuring that the proper voltages are delivered when needed.  In addition, the efficiency of electric motors is being improved further by introducing copper into the rotor as opposed to aluminium.  Meanwhile, in the developing economies, demand growth will mainly stem from increased consumption of electrical goods as disposable incomes rise. 

Copper’s third largest consuming sector, industrial machinery and equipment, accounts for 13% of total consumption. Both copper wire and cable and semi products supply this sector which includes equipment and machinery, industrial valves and fittings, off-highway vehicles and heat exchangers.  Copper wire and copper and copper alloy products are also used in transportation equipment, copper’s fourth largest category.  This includes the automotive, marine and aircraft/aerospace sectors.  It is within the automotive sector that developments of new copper applications have been most concentrated in recent years.  Prior to 1930 copper and brass, having excellent pressure containing and anticorrosion characteristics, were the favoured materials to be used in brake tubing.  However, mass auto production in the 1940s led to the adoption of furnace-brazed steel tubing because it was much lower in cost.  Although this form of tubing is still widely used today, copper has re-gained some of its lost market share through the introduction of a copper-nickel alloy (90% copper/10% nickel) which is more resistant to corrosion from road mud and salt than steel piping.  Likewise, new technology has led to the development of a new brazed copper-brass automotive radiator which has the necessary requirements to recapture some of the market share displaced by aluminium over the past twenty years. 

Meanwhile, 42-volt systems, hybrid vehicles and numerous electrical and electronic applications provide additional growth prospects for the use of copper within the automotive sector Over the years the number of electrical and electronic components installed per unit has been rising steadily, thereby creating the need for growth in the power and signal distribution system (otherwise known as the wiring harness).  Many of the electrical components will have to be redesigned in order to work effectively with the higher-voltage systems which could result in the copper content of some of the electrical components falling, but as more power becomes available, new electrical components will emerge.  Such examples include electronic valve actuation and electric braking, resulting in several kilos of copper, per unit, being added.  Forecasts have shown that over the next ten years, increases per vehicle will outweigh the decreases in copper required per component. 

Copper’s final end-use category is consumer and general products

. Copper consumed in this sector accounts for 8% of total copper consumption. The three main end-uses are electrical appliances, military ordnance and coinage. The production of the new Euro coin in recent years has helped to support demand for copper and copper alloy products.
